subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Supernovae and Life on Earth
description: A short lesson to help you apply Supernovae and Life on Earth.

hook.text: A nearby supernova could devastate life on Earth. But distant ones may have helped shape our evolution.

buildup.text: A supernova within 30 light-years could strip Earth's ozone layer, exposing life to deadly ultraviolet radiation.

discovery.text: Iron-60 isotopes found in deep-sea crusts show that supernovae exploded near Earth 2-3 million years ago.

twist.text: Some scientists link these nearby blasts to a minor extinction event and increased cosmic rays that may have altered evolution.

climax.text: Betelgeuse, 650 light-years away, will explode someday. It will be spectacular but far too distant to harm us.

punchline.text: Close supernovae threaten. Distant ones inspire. Betelgeuse will put on a show, safely.

quiz.question: How do scientists know supernovae exploded near Earth millions of years ago?
options: Iron-60 isotopes from supernova debris were found in deep-sea crusts on Earth
Ancient cave paintings depict bright stellar explosions in the sky
The Moon's craters show evidence of supernova shockwave impacts

details.summary: Every atom of calcium, iron, and oxygen in your body was forged in a supernova. These titanic explosions not only scatter heavy elements through space but may have directly influenced Earth's history — nearby supernovae have been linked to mass extinctions and changes in Earth's climate.
details.whyItMatters: Supernovae connect cosmic violence to the conditions for life. Without them, planets and biology couldn't exist. Understanding their impact on Earth links astrophysics to geology and evolutionary biology.
takeaways: Heavy elements essential for life were forged in supernovae
Nearby explosions may have influenced Earth's climate and extinctions
Supernovae are necessary precursors to rocky planet formation

faq.question: Have nearby supernovae affected Earth in the past?
faq.answer: Evidence suggests yes. Iron-60, a radioactive isotope produced only in supernovae, has been found in deep ocean sediments dating to 2-3 million years ago. This coincides with climate shifts and possibly the Pliocene-Pleistocene extinction.

faq.question: What elements do supernovae create?
faq.answer: Core-collapse supernovae produce elements from silicon through nickel during the explosion, plus heavier elements through rapid neutron capture (r-process). They scatter carbon, oxygen, silicon, iron, and traces of everything up to uranium.
